meta.title: Python DSA Interview Mastery Handbook
meta.subtitle: Data Structures + Problem-Solving Patterns + Ordered LeetCode Practice
meta.core_rule: Do not memorize complete solutions. Memorize the small reusable operations and learn to recognize when a problem is asking you to combine them.

learning_loop: Draw the data structure or state before coding.
Name the invariant: what must remain true after every iteration or recursive call?
Write the brute-force idea in one or two sentences.
Identify the bottleneck and choose the pattern that removes it.
Implement from a small template, not from a memorized full solution.
Trace one normal case and at least two edge cases.
Re-code the solution from memory the next day.
Revisit difficult problems after 3 days, 1 week, and 2 weeks.

topics.title: Arrays & Strings
topics.goal: Become completely comfortable with indexing, traversal, in-place updates, prefix/suffix information, sorting, and using an array as the state for other patterns.
what_to_master: Index safely and distinguish value vs index.
Traverse forward, backward, and with enumerate().
Modify an array in place with read/write pointers.
Use prefix sums for repeated range queries.
Use prefix/suffix products or extrema when each answer depends on everything except the current position.
Sort when ordering makes relationships easier to detect.
Understand O(1) extra-space vs creating a result array.
Recognize matrix/grid indexing as an extension of array indexing.
recognition_signals: Input is an array/string and the task asks for counts, ranges, subarrays, rearrangement, or in-place modification.
Repeated sum over ranges -> prefix sum.
Need all elements except self -> prefix/suffix.
Sorted result or easier neighbor comparison -> sorting may simplify the problem.
Contiguous portion of an array -> sliding window, prefix sum, or DP may be layered on top.

templates.name: Traversal + index
templates.note: This is the base operation behind almost every array technique.

templates.name: Prefix sum
templates.note: The extra leading zero eliminates special handling for ranges starting at index 0.
templates.code:
prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + x

# inclusive range [left, right]
range_sum = prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]

templates.name: In-place read/write pointer
templates.note: Use when the output can overwrite processed positions.

templates.name: Prefix/suffix product
templates.note: A powerful way to answer each position using information on both sides without division.
templates.code:
n = len(nums)
ans = [1] * n
prefix = 1
for i in range(n):
    ans[i] = prefix
    prefix *= nums[i]

suffix = 1
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    ans[i] *= suffix
    suffix *= nums[i]
return ans

common_mistakes: Off-by-one errors in range endpoints.
Confusing subarray (contiguous) with subsequence (not necessarily contiguous).
Mutating an array while still needing overwritten values.
Using nested loops before asking whether accumulated state can remove repeated work.

templates.name: Prefix state frequency
templates.note: This is the canonical prefix-sum + hash-map counting template.
templates.code:
count = 0
prefix = 0
freq = {0: 1}
for x in nums:
    prefix += x
    count += freq.get(prefix - k, 0)

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.goal: Control two indices or references so a quadratic search collapses into a linear scan whenever monotonic structure exists.
what_to_master: Opposite-end pointers on sorted data.
Same-direction read/write pointers.
Fast/slow pointers for linked structures.
Pointer movement based on an invariant, not guessing.
Know when sorting first enables two pointers.
Avoid re-checking regions already proven impossible.
recognition_signals: Sorted array + pair/triplet target.
Palindrome or symmetric comparison.
In-place removal/deduplication.
Need to shrink from both ends.
Linked-list middle/cycle -> fast/slow variant.
Brute force tests all pairs but moving one side can rule out many candidates.

templates.name: Opposite ends
templates.note: Correct only when pointer movement has a monotonic reason, usually sorted order.

templates.name: Read/write
templates.note: Use when compressing or rearranging in place.

templates.name: Palindrome scan
templates.note: A clean example of symmetric pointer convergence.
templates.code:
left, right = 0, len(s) - 1
while left < right:
    if s[left] != s[right]:
        return False
    left += 1
    right -= 1
return True

common_mistakes: Applying two pointers to unsorted data without a valid movement rule.
Moving both pointers when only one side has been proven impossible.
For 3Sum, forgetting duplicate skipping after sorting.

topics.graduation_requirement: You can state why moving the left or right pointer cannot discard a valid better answer. If you cannot explain that invariant, you are not yet using two pointers safely.

topics.title: Sliding Window
topics.goal: Solve contiguous subarray/substring problems by maintaining exactly the information needed for a moving range.
what_to_master: Fixed-size windows.
Variable-size windows that expand and shrink.
Maintain window sum/counts without recomputing.
Know the condition that makes a window valid or invalid.
Use frequency dictionaries for character windows.
Distinguish "longest valid" from "shortest valid" update timing.
Recognize when negative numbers break a standard monotonic window and prefix sums are needed instead.
recognition_signals: Longest/shortest contiguous substring or subarray.
At most / at least / exactly K conditions.
Repeatedly recomputing information for adjacent ranges.
String frequency or uniqueness condition over a contiguous window.
Positive numbers + minimum length target often enables shrink-while-valid.

templates.name: Fixed window
templates.note: Every step removes exactly one old element and adds one new element.
templates.code:
window_sum = sum(nums[:k])
best = window_sum
for right in range(k, len(nums)):
    window_sum += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
    best = max(best, window_sum)

templates.name: Variable window
templates.note: Canonical template for longest valid windows.
templates.code:
left = 0
for right in range(len(nums)):
    add(nums[right])

    while window_is_invalid():
        remove(nums[left])
        left += 1

    best = max(best, right - left + 1)

templates.name: Frequency window
templates.note: The window itself is represented by counts rather than slicing strings.
templates.code:
from collections import defaultdict
count = defaultdict(int)
left = 0
for right, ch in enumerate(s):
    count[ch] += 1
    while count[ch] > 1:
        count[s[left]] -= 1
        left += 1
    best = max(best, right - left + 1)

common_mistakes: Using slicing inside every iteration and accidentally making the algorithm O(n*k).
Updating a minimum answer after the window becomes invalid instead of while it is valid.
Using standard positive-number shrinking logic when negative values destroy monotonicity.
topics.graduation_requirement: You can write fixed and variable window templates from memory and, before coding, say what enters the window, what leaves, and the exact validity condition.

topics.title: Stacks
topics.goal: Use LIFO state to model nested structure, undo behavior, previous unresolved elements, and monotonic relationships.
what_to_master: Push/pop/peek in Python with a list.
Match nested delimiters.
Store indices when distance matters.
Use a monotonic increasing or decreasing stack.
Understand "next greater/smaller" and "previous greater/smaller."
Simulate recursion when appropriate.
Evaluate postfix expressions.
recognition_signals: Nested parentheses/brackets/tags.
Need the most recent unmatched item.
Next greater/smaller element.
Daily temperatures / stock span / histogram.
Undo/backtracking-like linear history.

templates.name: Basic stack
templates.note: Python lists provide efficient append/pop at the end.
templates.code:
stack = []
stack.append(value)
top = stack[-1]
value = stack.pop()

templates.name: Matching delimiters
templates.note: The top of the stack is the only opening token that can legally match next.

templates.name: Monotonic stack
templates.note: Items stay unresolved until the current value provides their answer.
templates.code:
stack = []  # indices, values decreasing
answer = [-1] * len(nums)
for i, x in enumerate(nums):
    while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < x:
        j = stack.pop()
        answer[j] = x
    stack.append(i)

common_mistakes: Storing values when the answer requires index distance.
Popping without checking whether the stack is empty.
Memorizing "increasing/decreasing" terminology instead of asking which unresolved elements should remain on the stack.
topics.graduation_requirement: You can identify what each stack entry represents and whether the stack is monotonic by value or by some derived property.

recognition_signals: First-in-first-out processing.

templates.name: FIFO queue
templates.note: Deque popleft() is O(1), unlike removing index 0 from a list.

what_to_master: Understand ListNode, head, next, and None.

recognition_signals: Head may change -> dummy node.
Middle/cycle -> fast and slow.

templates.name: ListNode + traversal
templates.note: Always be precise about whether a variable stores a node reference or a value.

templates.name: Dummy node
templates.note: Dummy nodes remove special-case logic when the head can change.
templates.code:
dummy = ListNode(0, head)
prev = dummy
curr = head
# modify using prev/curr
return dummy.next

templates.name: Reverse
templates.note: SAVE -> REVERSE -> MOVE prev -> MOVE curr.
templates.code:
prev = None
curr = head
while curr:
    nxt = curr.next
    curr.next = prev
    prev = curr
    curr = nxt
return prev

templates.name: Fast/slow middle
templates.note: When fast finishes, slow is around the middle.
templates.code:
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
return slow

templates.name: Merge two sorted lists
templates.note: Attach one node at a time while preserving both remaining suffixes.

common_mistakes: Changing curr.next before saving the original next node.
Returning dummy instead of dummy.next.
Comparing node objects when you intended to compare node values.
Failing to reconnect the prefix/suffix after a partial reversal.
combination_skills: Reorder List = middle + split + reverse + alternating merge.
LRU Cache = hash map + doubly linked list + sentinels.
topics.graduation_requirement: On a blank screen you can implement reverse(head), find_middle(head), merge(a,b), delete using a dummy node, and detect a cycle, and you can trace every pointer without losing the remaining list.

templates.name: Kahn topological sort
templates.note: A directed cycle prevents all vertices from reaching indegree zero.
templates.code:
from collections import deque
indegree = [0] * n
graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
for u, v in edges:
    graph[u].append(v)
    indegree[v] += 1
q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indegree[i] == 0)
order = []
while q:
    u = q.popleft(); order.append(u)
    for v in graph[u]:
        indegree[v] -= 1
        if indegree[v] == 0:
            q.append(v)
return order if len(order) == n else []

topics.title: Backtracking
topics.goal: Explore a decision tree by choosing, recursing, and undoing; generate combinations/permutations or search constrained possibilities.
what_to_master: Define the decision state.
Choose -> recurse -> undo.
Identify a base case that records a complete answer.
Avoid duplicate work through sorting/skipping or used sets.
Prune branches that cannot produce valid results.
Distinguish subsets, combinations, permutations, and partitioning.
recognition_signals: Generate all subsets/permutations/combinations.
Need all possible valid arrangements.

Input size is small enough for exponential exploration.

templates.name: Generic backtracking
templates.note: The defining feature is restoration of state after exploring a branch.
templates.code:
result = []
path = []

def backtrack(state):
    if complete(state):
        result.append(path.copy())
        return

    for choice in choices(state):
        if not valid(choice, state):
            continue
        path.append(choice)
        apply(choice, state)
        backtrack(state)
        undo(choice, state)
        path.pop()

templates.name: Subsets
templates.note: Every partial path is itself a valid subset.

templates.name: Permutations
templates.note: Each position can choose any not-yet-used element.

common_mistakes: Appending path instead of path.copy(), causing all saved answers to reference the same mutable list.
Using a global visited set when cells/values should only be blocked within the current path.
Failing to sort/skip duplicates for duplicate-sensitive combination problems.
topics.graduation_requirement: You can draw the decision tree for subsets, combinations, and permutations and explain exactly what state must be undone after each recursive call.

topics.title: Greedy Algorithms
topics.goal: Make a locally optimal choice only when you can justify that it never blocks a globally optimal solution.
what_to_master: Identify a safe local choice.
Sort by the property that exposes the greedy invariant.
Use exchange arguments conceptually: any optimal solution can be transformed to include your greedy choice.
Track only necessary state instead of all possibilities.
Know when a greedy-looking approach fails and DP is needed.
recognition_signals: Minimize number of intervals/resources.
Scheduling and non-overlap.
Choose farthest/earliest/cheapest next action with provable safety.
Need global optimum but local decisions have a dominance property.
If choices have long-term interacting consequences, be suspicious and consider DP.

templates.name: Interval greedy
templates.note: Choosing the earliest finishing compatible interval leaves the most room for future choices.

templates.name: Reachability greedy
templates.note: Maintain the strongest reachable frontier; dominated paths do not need separate state.

common_mistakes: Calling an algorithm greedy merely because it uses one pass.
Using greedy when current decisions alter future options in a way that requires remembering multiple states.
Sorting by the wrong interval endpoint/property.

topics.graduation_requirement: For every greedy solution, you can explain why a different local choice cannot lead to a strictly better future outcome. "It seems optimal" is not enough.

topics.title: Divide & Conquer
topics.goal: Split a problem into smaller independent instances, solve them recursively, and combine their results efficiently.
what_to_master: Base case, divide, conquer, combine.
Merge sort on arrays and linked lists.
Binary-search family as divide-and-conquer intuition.
Tree recursion as structural decomposition.
Know when subproblems overlap: if heavily overlapping, memoization/DP may be better.
recognition_signals: Problem naturally splits into independent halves.
Need sort/merge behavior.
Each recursive half can be solved without sharing mutable state.
Combining solutions is cheaper than solving the whole problem directly.

templates.name: Merge sort
templates.note: The combine step determines the overall efficiency; merge is linear.

templates.name: Generic divide/conquer
templates.note: Use when the subproblems are mostly independent rather than repeatedly overlapping.

common_mistakes: Creating costly slices in Python without considering space/time impact.
Recursing without a shrinking problem size/base case.
Labeling DP as divide-and-conquer even when the same subproblems are recomputed many times.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming
topics.goal: Turn overlapping recursive choices into reusable states; learn to design state, transition, base cases, evaluation order, and space optimization.
what_to_master: Recursion tree and overlapping subproblems.
Memoization (top-down).
Tabulation (bottom-up).
Define state in a complete sentence.
Write transition from smaller states.
Choose base cases.
1D DP, 2D/grid DP, knapsack/subset DP, sequence DP, interval DP.
Space optimization when only previous rows/states are needed.
Recognize DP vs greedy vs backtracking.
recognition_signals: Count number of ways.
Maximum/minimum over many choices with overlapping suffix/prefix states.
"At each position choose take/skip."
Grid paths/cost.
Sequence alignment, subsequence, edit operations.
Capacity/target subset problems.
Brute-force recursion repeats the same arguments.

templates.name: Top-down memoization
templates.note: Start from a natural recursion; cache answers by the complete state.

templates.name: Bottom-up 1D
templates.note: Compute states only after every dependency is already known.
templates.code:
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
dp[0] = base
for i in range(1, n + 1):
    dp[i] = transition(dp, i)
return dp[n]

templates.name: Two-row sequence DP
templates.note: Typical for LCS-style DP. Allocate a fresh current row or correctly reset reused state.

templates.name: 0/1 knapsack direction
templates.note: Iterating backward ensures each item is used at most once.

common_mistakes: Defining a state that does not contain enough information to determine future decisions.
Writing a recurrence before stating what dp means.
Using prev = cur with a reused mutable row and accidentally reading values from the current iteration.
Using forward iteration for 0/1 knapsack and unintentionally reusing an item multiple times.
combination_skills: Backtracking explores the full decision tree; memoized DP collapses repeated states.
Greedy keeps one dominant state only when a proof shows alternatives are unnecessary.
Binary search can optimize some DP-like sequence problems such as LIS, but it changes the meaning of the maintained array.
topics.graduation_requirement: Before touching code you can answer five questions: (1) What does dp(state) mean? (2) What choices exist? (3) What smaller states are needed? (4) What are the base cases? (5) In what order can states be computed?

decision_tree.question: Need fast lookup, duplicates, counts, grouping?
Nested structure / next greater / unresolved previous items?
Middle/cycle/Nth from end in linked list?

Safe locally optimal choice with proof?

steps: Restate the input, output, constraints, and one example in your own words.
Ask whether order, duplicates, mutation, and extra space matter if the prompt is ambiguous.
State a brute-force solution and its complexity. This gives you a correctness baseline.
Locate the bottleneck: repeated lookup, repeated range work, repeated state, or exhaustive search.
Match the bottleneck to a pattern from the decision tree.
State your invariant or DP state before coding.
Code the smallest reusable operations first.
Trace the provided example plus an edge case: empty/singleton, duplicates, boundary value, cycle, disconnected component, etc.
State time and space complexity and identify any Python-specific cost such as slicing or recursion depth.
interview_workflow.key_habit: Do not say "I think this is sliding window" and immediately code. Say what the window represents and why advancing/shrinking preserves correctness. The same rule applies to every pattern.

daily_practice_format: 10 minutes: re-code yesterday's core template without notes.
20-30 minutes: attempt one new problem without solution help.
10 minutes: compare with the official/editorial approach and identify the missing insight.
15-25 minutes: solve or re-solve a second problem that uses the same pattern.
5 minutes: write one sentence: "I should recognize this pattern when..."
readiness_test: You can solve most Easy problems in your mastered topics in 10-15 minutes.
You can usually classify a Medium problem into 1-2 likely patterns within 3-5 minutes.
You can write the core template without syntax searching.
You can explain time and space complexity before finishing the code.
You recover from pointer/index mistakes by tracing state rather than restarting randomly.
You can solve mixed sets without knowing the tagged topic in advance.
